source.title: Data-centric NLP Backdoor Defense from the Lens of Memorization
source.authors: Zhen-Ting Wang; Zhizhi Wang; Ming-Yu Jin; Meng-Nan Du; Juan Zhai; Shi-Qing Ma

record.file_problem: Text includes the full paper and appendices; no truncation or garbling apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and empirically examines a different memorization/generalization relationship: duplication of poisoned trigger elements and backdoor success. It does not test the listed natural-label generalization versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that attack success rates rise with the number of poisoning samples for BadNets and AddSent (Figure 3; described in Appendix B). Defense BA/ASR tables concern deliberately induced backdoor behavior and do not measure the natural-label generalization gap in the listed versions. Other reported defense, detection, and efficiency results are not rows for this claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures deliberately induced NLP backdoors and defense performance. Its trigger-duplication experiments and theoretical bound do not test any of V1–V8. Citing Feldman and Zhang's memorization definition does not test or use V8's example-removal finding.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors define backdoors as element-wise memorization, attribute stronger backdoor learning to trigger duplication, and use this account to motivate a data-centric defense. They additionally claim duplication is necessary for successful attacks; their empirical evidence establishes the reported trend in the tested settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines poisoned NLP classification and generative tasks, relating trigger duplication to backdoor behavior; it does not use the natural-label generalization setups in the claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: For BERT on SST-2, BadNets and AddSent ASR increases with poisoning-sample count; Appendix B reports ASR below 50% with 1–25 poisoning samples. This measures deliberately induced trigger learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing trigger duplication through additional poisoned training samples increases backdoor success in these tested NLP attacks.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The empirical trigger-duplication relationship is shown only in Figure 3, without numerical values or reported uncertainty. The theorem proof states assumptions including a finite model parameter set and samples drawn from the general distribution.
record.rows_left_out: Defense BA/ASR results in Tables 1–2, 4, 6, 8–10, and 12 concern the performance of defenses against deliberately poisoned backdoor tasks; they do not measure any listed natural-label generalization version. Trigger-detection precision/recall and runtime results likewise do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning and optimizer modifications.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout's effects on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing examples ranked by sample-wise label memorization versus removing equally many random examples, followed by retraining and test-accuracy comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Removing trigger-containing poisoned samples is not V8's removal of examples ranked by their inclusion's effect on predicting their own labels. The defense tables also lack V8's matched random-removal comparison. No additional results bearing on V1–V8 require rows.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization; the listed architectures and training recipes.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected image models and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning or optimizer changes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out natural-label error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the natural-label generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting natural-label test accuracy.
